description: COSMIC HEARTH is a team brought together by our shared curiosity about space and our interest in solving problems together. We bring different strengths in research, data analysis, and problem-solving. After participating in the 2025 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are returning this year with more curiosity, interest, and dedication. We look forward to exploring new ideas and creating something we can be proud of.
summary:
Humanity’s next giant leap to the Moon and Mars starts right here on Earth. We developed TERRA ANALOG, an interactive web platform featuring 27 verified Earth analog sites, including 16 lunar and 11 Martian locations. It includes an interactive map, custom planetary filters, and a community registration tool that allows users to submit new coordinates and instantly calculate similarity scores and add new pins onto the map.

Each location is assigned a quantitative similarity score based on its comparison with real lunar and Martian targets. By evaluating key environmental metrics alongside protected ecological zones and planetary conditions that cannot be fully replicated on Earth, the platform provides a clearer picture of how closely each terrestrial site resembles conditions beyond Earth.

More than just a database, TERRA ANALOG brings global data together in one platform, helping engineers and researchers identify suitable locations to test rovers, drills, and habitats on Earth before using them in missions to other worlds.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
TERRA ANALOG is an interactive web platform built to compare 27 real locations on Earth (16 for the Moon and 11 for Mars) that share environmental and geological traits with both worlds.

The main screen is a dark world map with color-coded pins for lunar (cyan) and Martian (orange) analog sites. When a user clicks a pin, the map zooms in on that location and opens a side panel with site photos, a short field summary, and similarity scores across four categories: Surface Temperature, Terrain Slope, Geology and Regolith, and Water Ice or Subsurface Features. Users can filter pins by planet (All, Moon, or Mars) and save locations to a personal mission list. The platform also includes a comparison table so users can evaluate multiple analog sites side by side across key planetary metrics.

What benefits and intended impact does it have?
Space agencies and engineering teams test rovers, spacesuits, ground-penetrating radar, drills, and habitats at Earth analog sites before launching hardware to space. Right now, planetary orbital data is spread across technical archives, and most studies focus repeatedly on the same few locations.

TERRA ANALOG puts NASA orbital baselines, terrain metrics, and site comparisons into one simple map interface. Our goal is to help engineers and researchers quickly find the right Earth environment for specific hardware tests (like lava tubes for GPS-denied navigation or hyper-arid permafrost valleys for ice drilling).

What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did we use?

  • Lunar Data and Tools: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) datasets accessed through the PDS Lunar Orbital Data Explorer (ODE) and LROC QuickMap, using LOLA altimetry and slope maps alongside Diviner thermal and rock abundance layers.
  • Martian Data and Tools: NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), MRO HiRISE high-resolution imagery, NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS), USGS EarthExplorer (Landsat imagery and elevation models), European Space Agency (ESA) datasets, QGIS, and Google Earth Pro for terrain and slope profiles.
  • Earth Data: NASA Earthdata Worldview (Terra/MODIS Land Surface Temperature, Days with Snow Cover, and Blue Marble Shaded Relief).
  • Web Development: Built with the Astro framework, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, bundled with Vite and managed with pnpm. We stored the planetary analog dataset in structured JSON files, used Leaflet with Carto dark map tiles for the interactive map and zoom transitions, and used browser LocalStorage to save user missions without a paid backend.

How is our project creative?
We wanted to move away from static spreadsheets and build an interactive tool with four main features:

  1. Mission-Control Map Experience: We designed a single-screen dark interface with smooth camera zoom transitions and floating telemetry panels, turning a plain database into an interactive planetary navigation tool.
  2. Combined Multi-Planet Scoring System: We paired a mathematical normalization formula for numerical satellite measurements (temperature and slope) with two independent four-level rubrics for qualitative field conditions (geology and ice or cave stability). This lets users evaluate both lunar and Martian regions under one consistent standard, and when a site lacks local weather station temperature records (marked as N/A), the system averages the remaining three metrics so incomplete data does not skew the final score.
  3. Zero-Backend Sustainable Architecture: By combining structured JSON datasets, open Leaflet and Carto map layers, and browser LocalStorage, the entire platform runs fast and lets users explore and save custom missions with zero server or API costs.
  4. Global Site Diversity: Alongside well-known benchmarks, we researched 27 diverse sites worldwide. For the Moon, we included Tso Kar Basin (India), Okmok Caldera (Alaska), and the Santa Cruz Lava Tubes (Galápagos, Ecuador). For Mars, we included Qaidam Basin (China), University Valley and Lake Vida (Antarctica), Bockfjord Volcanic Complex (Svalbard), Askja Volcano (Iceland), Dallol (Ethiopia), Haughton Crater (Canada), and Río Tinto (Spain).

What factors did our team consider?

  • Orbital Baseline Accuracy: Every comparison uses real spacecraft measurements as its reference target. For the Moon, we separated the steep, ice-bearing Lunar South Pole, the flat basaltic Lunar Maria, and the Marius Hills lava tubes (from LRO LOLA and Diviner data). For Mars, we compared against Gale Crater, Medusae Fossae, Meridiani Planum, and Martian permafrost and impact terrains (from MRO HiRISE, NASA PDS, NTRS, and ESA data).
  • Exact Coordinates and Local Scale: We scored specific craters, calderas, dry lakebeds, valleys, and lava tubes rather than broad countries or regions, using verified coordinates and slope profiles from LROC QuickMap, NASA Earthdata Worldview, USGS EarthExplorer, Google Earth Pro, and QGIS.
  • Terrestrial Limitations: Every site profile lists what Earth cannot reproduce, including 1/6 lunar gravity, 1/3 Martian gravity, hard vacuum, extreme day-night temperature swings, and cosmic radiation, so teams know the physical limits of each testbed.
  • Protected Areas and Field Ethics: Several analog sites in our database sit inside protected regions, including the Santa Cruz Lava Tubes (Galápagos National Park, Ecuador), Tso Kar Basin (Ramsar Wetland, India), University Valley and Lake Vida (Antarctic Specially Managed Area), and Tnorala or Gosses Bluff (conservation and Indigenous sacred site, Australia). We noted these protections to remind teams that real fieldwork requires environmental permits and non-invasive testing.

Future Improvements
Due to hackathon time constraints, we focused on delivering a verified baseline of 27 global sites. Next, we plan to expand the platform with five features:

  • AI Mission Objective Recommender: An intelligent assistant where engineers describe their specific test goals (such as subsurface ice drilling, rover traction, or habitat shielding) and receive ranked analog site recommendations with technical explanations.
  • Community Site Submission Form: An interactive form where researchers and users can input temperature, slope, and field conditions to calculate similarity scores and add new analog pins directly to the map.
  • Automated Engineering Readiness Checklists: Rule-based recommendations that automatically flag required rover or habitat equipment (such as thermal heaters or high-slope suspension) based on a selected site's extreme metrics.
  • 3D Terrain Elevation Overlays: Integrating 3D topographic models from QGIS and NASA DEM datasets so engineers can inspect crater slopes and lava tube entrances before field deployment.
